name: Anti-communism
summary: Anti-communism is active opposition to communism, its parties and the states it governed. Reference works describe it as a 'broad church' running from socialists and social democrats through liberals and conservatives to the far right, united in holding communism a threat to be contained or defeated and divided on almost everything else. In its main Cold War form it defended liberal democracy and market economies against Soviet power through alliances such as NATO, foreign aid, military build-up, propaganda and covert action, and at home through loyalty checks and, in West Germany, a ban on the Communist Party.
scope: As the defining sources set it out: Scott-Smith's reference entry (Encyclopedia of Modern Europe, s5) treats anticommunism as a broad church of socialists, liberals and social democrats, conservatives, the far right and the left opposition, with its Cold War struggle bound up with liberal democracy and capitalism; Heineman's entry (Americans at War, s7) traces American anticommunism from the Red Scare through the Truman Doctrine, NSC 68, McCarthyism and the Reagan Doctrine; Gerth (s9) defines it as a creed that holds communism a supreme evil its followers seek to impose on the world. The profile answers from these sources, from the two primary texts they tie to it (the Truman Doctrine, s2, and NSC 68, s10, both named in s7), and, for record over words, from the anticommunist acts these references report (s6, s8): bans and loyalty checks, NATO, aid, covert operations and armed support for insurgents. Where the sources show the camp divided on a statement it is 0 at low confidence, and where they are silent it is null. Positions that belong to the ideologies within the camp (Catholic social teaching, Hayek's liberalism, fascism) are not anti-communism's own unless these sources present them as such, and the narrower national anticommunisms (British, South Korean, Taiwanese) are other subjects.

sources.title: Anticommunism

sources.usedFor: Defining source: anticommunism as a 'broad church' from left to right (socialists, liberals/social democrats, conservatives, far right, left opposition); the Cold War struggle for liberal democracy and capitalism; welfare-state consensus versus conservatives; antitotalitarianism, Hayek, the Congress for Cultural Freedom and the 'End of Ideology'; Christianity as a source. sources.title: Anticommunism (the record it reports)
sources.author: Giles Scott-Smith, Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: Europe Since 1914 (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Acts it reports: the KPD ban (1956) and loyalty checks, exclusion of communist parties from government, the Marshall Plan and NATO, CIA-funded guerrillas, fronts and radio, Gladio and the Strategy of Tension, NATO missile deployment.

sources.title: Communism and Anticommunism
sources.author: Kenneth J. Heineman, Americans at War (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Defining source for American anticommunism: the Truman Doctrine and containment, NSC 68 and rollback, the horseshoe view of communism and Nazism, McCarthyism, Reagan's rejection of coexistence. Read in full.

sources.title: Communism and Anticommunism (the record it reports)
sources.author: Kenneth J. Heineman, Americans at War (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Acts it reports: the adoption of NSC 68, the Reagan Doctrine's support for anticommunist fighters, CIA covert and insurgency campaigns, US efforts to recruit allies, the secret Cuba-Turkey missile provision, SALT and detente, the arms race.

sources.title: Anti-Communism in Britain During the Early Cold War: A Very British Witch Hunt
sources.author: Matthew Gerth (University of London Press, 2023, open access)
sources.usedFor: Only its section 'Defining anti-communism' (Introduction): the tenets that communism is a supreme evil its followers seek to impose on the world, the Manichaean crusade view, and anti-communism as a defender of the traditional social order. Its findings on Britain describe a narrower subject and are not used.

sources.title: NSC 68: United States Objectives and Programs for National Security
sources.author: US National Security Council (14 April 1950), FAS copy
sources.usedFor: The free society against the 'slave state', the individual as an end in himself, minority rights, rejection of isolation, military build-up, atomic weapons, covert measures, trade policy. Heineman (s7) names it as the policy that took anticommunism from containment to rollback. Read in full.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-08), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-15) answered mostly from Wikipedia, Divini Redemptoris and the SEP entry on Hayek, and recorded a range of positions across the camp as 0. Under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence; the encyclical and Hayek are Catholic social teaching's and liberalism's own texts, not tied to anti-communism by its defining sources (no coatrack); so each first-pass answer was re-answered from the sources below or nulled, with the first version kept in its reviewHistory (s1, s3 and s4 stay listed for that history). This pass read in full the Scott-Smith and Heineman reference entries, the Truman Doctrine and NSC 68, and the definitional part of Gerth's introduction. Themes searched: economy (welfare state, planning, trade), government (democracy, party bans, minority rights), liberty and society (individual, religion), world (alliances, aid, covert action, nuclear weapons, intervention) and means (violence, revolution). The sources describe anti-communism as a cross-spectrum stance, so most domestic questions (healthcare, taxes, unions, family, sexuality, immigration, ecology, technology) stay null: the defining sources either say nothing or describe the camp's members disagreeing in general terms. After the first draft failed the uncertainty rule on lines 9 (gender and family), 11 (minorities and secession), 5 (race) and 8 (nationalism), these themes were searched again: the defining sources and the Americans at War entry 'Americanism vs. Godless Communism' say nothing that settles them, and the scholarship found (Lewis on southern segregationists' use of anticommunism, Bernini on family propaganda in Catholic Italy and Poland) is about other subjects using anticommunism, so it was not used (no coatrack). Not reached: the Springer Open special issue on anticommunism (Asian Journal of German and European Studies, 2017) and the core.ac.uk copy refuse scripted access (bot check, 403); the OAPEN catalogue refuses scripted search (403); Powers, Not Without Honor, and the Palgrave volume Transnational Anti-Communism and the Cold War are not open access. A state where anti-communism was the official doctrine (South Korea's 1961 'anti-communism as the first national policy') would count as its record, but no accessible defining source documents it.
